problem_text: Suppose you are chosen as a technology assistant by the director of the opening ceremony for the 2022 Winter Olympics, and your job is to evaluate the program proposals. One of the backup programs is a skating show of a ensemble of drones dressed as mascots, which are moving along a circle. Since the number of the drones is sufficiently large, we can use a probability density function rho(t, v)(>=0) to represent the distribution of the drones. Here v in R is the line speed, and for a given time t, and two speeds v1<v2, integral from v1 to v2 of rho(t,v)dv is the probability of finding a drone with its speed between v1 and v2. Suppose that the dynamics of the density function is governed by rho_t + ((u(t)-v)rho)_v = rho_vv, v in R, t>0, where u(t) is the command speed. (1) To investigate proper choices of the command speed, D.B. propose that we shall choose u(t) = u0 + u1*N(t) where u0>0, u1>0 and N(t) is the average of the positive part of the speed v+ = max{0,v}, i.e., N(t) = integral from 0 to infinity of v*rho(t,v)dv. But you claim that if u1>1, N(t) may become unbounded in evolution, such that the drones may be out of order. Can you prove it? (For simplicity, the contributions of rho and its derivatives at |v|->+infinity are neglected.) (2) After taking those advices, the director is wondering whether the drones will be evenly distributed along the circle. Thus, we shall consider the joint density function p(t,x,v)(>=0) of position and speed, where x in [0,2pi] is the position coordinate on the circle. Clearly, integral from 0 to 2pi of p(t,x,v)dx = rho(t,v). Suppose that the governing equation for p(t,x,v) is p_t + v*p_x + ((u(t)-v)p)_v = p_vv, x in [0,2pi], v in R, t>0. Because the drones are circulating around, the following boundary condition is satisfied: p(t,0,v) = p(t,2pi,v). You have a feeling that, no matter how the drones are distributed initially, they will become almost evenly distributed very quickly. Can you prove or disprove this statement?
solution_text: Part (1): Define M(t) = integral from -inf to +inf of v*rho(t,v)dv (the average speed). By direct calculation using the PDE and integration by parts (boundary terms vanish at infinity), dM/dt = u(t) - M(t) = u0 + u1*N(t) - M(t). Since M(t) = N(t) + integral from -inf to 0 of v*rho dv, and the second integral is <= 0 (v<0, rho>=0), we have M(t) <= N(t). Therefore dM/dt >= u0 + u1*M(t) - M(t) = u0 + (u1-1)*M(t). When u1 > 1, this differential inequality (Gronwall-type) implies M(t) grows at least exponentially, so M(t) -> +infinity. Since N(t) >= M(t), N(t) also diverges to +infinity. Part (2): Fourier decompose p(t,x,v) = sum_k p_k(t,v)*e^{ikx}. The k=0 mode satisfies the same equation as rho. For k!=0, the equation has an extra term ikv*p_k from advection. Define energy E_k(t) = integral of |p_k|^2 dv. Energy estimates show dE_k/dt involves -2*integral of |p_k_v|^2 dv (dissipation) which dominates, causing E_k(t) -> 0 for k!=0. Thus p(t,x,v) approaches (1/pi)*p_0(t,v), which is an even distribution in space.
solution_summary: Part 1: Define auxiliary quantity M(t)=∫vρ dv, derive ODE dM/dt=u₀+u₁N-M via integration by parts, use M≤N to get Gronwall inequality dM/dt≥u₀+(u₁-1)M, conclude exponential divergence when u₁>1. Part 2: Fourier decompose p in x, show k≠0 modes decay via energy estimates (dissipation dominates), leaving uniform spatial distribution.
answer: Part 1: When t→+∞, M(t)→+∞, therefore N(t) also diverges to +∞ (when u₁>1). Part 2: For k≠0, p_k(t,v) decays, and p(t,x,v) approaches (1/π)p_0(t,v), which is an even distribution in space.

rounds.question: Describe the structure of this problem. What are the key objects, what PDEs govern them, and what are you asked to prove in each part?
rounds.expected_answer: Two-part problem. Part 1: prove N(t)=∫₀^∞vρ dv diverges when u₁>1, where ρ satisfies transport-diffusion PDE ρ_t+((u-v)ρ)_v=ρ_vv and u(t)=u₀+u₁N(t). Part 2: prove p(t,x,v) becomes uniform in x on circle [0,2π], where p satisfies p_t+vp_x+((u-v)p)_v=p_vv with periodic BC.

rounds.question: What methods could you use to analyze the behavior of N(t)? List all approaches you can think of.
rounds.expected_answer: Direct computation of dN/dt, moment methods (define M(t)=∫vρ dv as auxiliary), energy estimates, comparison principles, Gronwall inequalities, Fourier analysis for Part 2.

rounds.question: Try computing dN/dt directly by differentiating N(t)=∫₀^∞vρ(t,v)dv and substituting the PDE. What happens?
rounds.expected_answer: dN/dt = ∫₀^∞vρ_t dv = ∫₀^∞v[-((u-v)ρ)_v+ρ_vv]dv. Integration by parts produces boundary terms at v=0 (from the half-line limit) that are hard to control. The direct approach gets stuck.

rounds.question: Instead of N(t), define M(t)=∫_{-∞}^{∞}vρ(t,v)dv (full average speed). Compute dM/dt using the PDE, integrating by parts. Use that boundary terms vanish at |v|→∞ and ∫ρdv=1.
rounds.expected_answer: dM/dt=∫vρ_t dv=∫v[-((u-v)ρ)_v+ρ_vv]dv=∫[(u-v)ρ-ρ_v]dv=u(t)∫ρdv-∫vρdv=u(t)-M(t)=u₀+u₁N(t)-M(t). Clean ODE with no boundary term issues.

rounds.question: You have dM/dt=u₀+u₁N(t)-M(t) but N(t) appears on the right. Find an inequality relating M(t) and N(t) to close this into a self-contained differential inequality, then apply Gronwall.
rounds.expected_answer: M(t)=N(t)+∫_{-∞}⁰vρdv≤N(t) since the second integral is ≤0. So dM/dt≥u₀+u₁M(t)-M(t)=u₀+(u₁-1)M(t). When u₁>1, Gronwall gives M(t)≥M(0)e^{(u₁-1)t}+u₀/(u₁-1)(e^{(u₁-1)t}-1)→+∞. Since N≥M, N(t)→+∞.

rounds.question: For Part 2, the domain is periodic in x∈[0,2π]. What decomposition is natural? Write the mode equations and identify what needs to be shown.
rounds.expected_answer: Fourier decompose p(t,x,v)=Σ_k p_k(t,v)e^{ikx}. k=0 mode satisfies same equation as ρ. For k≠0: p_k_t+ikv·p_k+((u-v)p_k)_v=p_k_vv. Need to show E_k(t)=∫|p_k|²dv→0 for k≠0, implying p→(1/2π)p_0 (uniform in x).

rounds.question: Complete the energy estimate for k≠0 modes. Compute dE_k/dt and show the dissipation term causes decay, concluding the drones become evenly distributed.
rounds.expected_answer: dE_k/dt=2Re∫p_k*p_k_t dv. After integration by parts: dE_k/dt=-2∫|p_k_v|²dv + (terms from advection/convection). The dissipation term -2∫|p_k_v|²dv≤0 dominates, showing E_k(t) is decreasing (or decays). Thus p_k→0 for k≠0, and p(t,x,v)→(1/π)p_0(t,v), uniform in x.
